title: Disinformation narratives in Spain: reach, impact and spreading patterns
screen_reason: Nationally distributed online survey of 1,003 Spanish residents (10-16 March 2022) in which respondents were asked, for each of six fact-checker-derived disinformation narratives, whether they had heard it before. Figure 1 gives the share of respondents answering Yes for each narrative (29.01% to 72.88%). These are self-reported exposure shares of a survey denominator, i.e. RECALL estimates.

estimates.platform: cross-media self-report (respondents named TV, social media and messaging apps, digital media, press, radio or public talk as the channel)
estimates.date: survey fielded 10-16 March 2022; narratives drawn from fact-checks published 14 February - 7 March 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had heard disinformation narrative N1 (Covid&WHO: Poland, Sweden and Norway have sued the WHO for infecting Europe) before the survey
estimates.value_raw: 29.01% 'Have you heard about it Yes' (Figure 1, narrative 1); reported in the text as 'heard by 29% of respondents'
estimates.denominator: 1,003 Spanish residents aged 18-74 (Gesop online panel, stratified by sex x age with 125 interviews per stratum, distributed proportionally by autonomous community and municipality size)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered Yes to 'has the respondent heard the narrative before' when presented with the narrative statement: 'Poland, Sweden and Norway have filed a lawsuit against the World Health Organization accusing it of infecting Europe.'
estimates.misinfo_def: "The field now uses the broadly accepted concept of disinformation, referring to false or misleading information that is deliberately spread through multiple platforms to deceive or manipulate public opinion."
estimates.source_quote: Just one of the narratives shows limited reach (N1-Covid&WHO), being heard by 29% of respondents.
estimates.page_loc: Section 4 Results, first paragraph; Figure 1 'Reach of disinformation narratives' (narrative 1: Yes 29.01, No 70, DNK/DNA 0.99)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure itself is self-reported: the respondent says whether they had heard the narrative before, with no behavioural verification. The stimulus, however, is fact-checker derived: 163 fact-checks published by the Spanish fact-checkers Newtral, Maldita and Verificat between 14 February and 7 March 2022 were logged daily and coded; two journalists from Newtral and two researchers coded and clustered them independently, then compared and reconciled over three days, agreeing on six narratives. No inter-coder reliability statistic is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The survey was launched on March 10th until 16th, online, with N=1.003, among Spanish residents between 18 and 74 years old, with a margin of error of +/- 3,4% for a confidence level of 95% and p=q=0,5. The survey company Gesop was hired to conduct the fieldwork, which was conducted with the usual stratified with uniform affixation sampling method.
estimates.notes: The six narrative rows all share the same 1,003-respondent denominator; only one of them (or their average) should enter any pooled prevalence analysis. The paper reports no pooled 'heard at least one narrative' figure. N1 is the only narrative whose reach is given verbatim in the running text (29%); the decimal value 29.01 comes from the Figure 1 data labels.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) No pooled 'heard at least one of the six narratives' figure is reported, and none was computed (that would be a cross-category combination, barred by R8). The six rows therefore share one denominator and should be treated as one study when pooling. (2) Table 2 (spreading channels: e.g. N4 TV 60.09%, N3 social media 41.36%) gives, for each narrative, the distribution of the channel through which those who heard it say they heard it. It is a within-exposed channel breakdown of an unstated sub-denominator (only the exposed answered), not a share of the population or of items, so no rows. It would, however, support a channel moderator if an adjudicator wants it. (3) Table 3 (trust on narratives: 22.13% to 52.14% 'Believing') is belief in false claims, explicitly out of scope. (4) Table 4 reports Cramer's V for the exposure-belief association, not a share. (5) The questionnaire asked whether respondents 'had they shared related content', but no sharing result is reported anywhere in the paper, so no RECALL-sharing row can be extracted; this is a visible reporting gap. (6) The 163 fact-checks collected are the sampling material for the narratives, not a denominator of content judged false. (7) Figure 1's values had to be read from OCR-garbled data labels; the assignment of each value to its narrative is corroborated by each triple summing to 100.0 and by the running text.

rob.design: Online survey of a commercial panel (Gesop), N = 1,003 Spanish residents aged 18-74, fielded 10-16 March 2022, stated margin of error +/-3.4% at 95% confidence; stratified with uniform affixation by sex x age (125 interviews in each of eight strata), distributed proportionally by autonomous community and municipality size; achieved 49% men / 51% women, age quartiles reported. No response or completion rate given, and the age bands reported (18-29, 30-44, 45-49, 60-74) do not tile the 18-74 range, which looks like a typographical error in the paper. Stimulus construction: 163 fact-checks from Newtral, Maldita and Verificat (14 February - 7 March 2022) coded daily into an Excel database; two Newtral journalists and two researchers coded and clustered independently, compared and agreed six narratives over three days; no kappa or agreement statistic reported. Analysis in R; chi-square and Cramer's V.
rob.item6_quote: The field now uses the broadly accepted concept of disinformation, referring to false or misleading information that is deliberately spread through multiple platforms to deceive or manipulate public opinion.
rob.item10_quote: Just one of the narratives shows limited reach (N1-Covid&WHO), being heard by 29% of respondents. Other two narratives (N3-MENAS and N5-CovidVaccines), related to immigration and covid-related disinformation, were spread among 60%. Despite being a high percentage, there were three other narratives that overpass 70% reach.
